lead: To understand why people act the way they do, look at what the rules are rewarding.
when: When what the rules say doesn't match how people actually behave, cooperation keeps relying on a few people carrying extra weight, or you're about to introduce rewards or performance reviews.
body:
A team says it values collaboration, but when it comes to praise and handing out opportunities, it only looks at how much each person gets done individually. If some people then don't want to spend time helping coworkers, it's not necessarily a lack of team spirit. They may simply be responding to the rules that actually count.

Incentives are the arrangements of rewards, costs, and rules that shape behavioral choices, including material gain, recognition, responsibility, relationships, and the consequences of actions.

Incentives aren't just bonuses. Being noticed, being trusted, avoiding hassle, protecting your reputation, and having room to choose can all shape behavior. The same arrangement can also affect different people differently, so you can't assume how people will respond based only on what the designer hopes.

The purpose of seeing incentives clearly is to bring the rules more in line with the behavior you really want to encourage, and to see who bears the costs and who gets the benefits. It's not about seeing everyone as only chasing their own interest, and it's certainly not about finding buttons to manipulate others.

The flowchart starts with the behavior you hope for, then the actual consequences, and then how people might choose next time. Marking who bears the costs and who gets the rewards makes it easier to see whether the rules are steering behavior toward the goal.
example:
A team wants members to share what they've learned in a timely way, but sharing takes preparation, presenting, and answering questions, and none of that time counts as part of the workload. People have to squeeze it into their free time, and over time the sessions become harder and harder to keep going.

First confirm that members actually need it, then make room for it during work hours, recognize specific contributions, and cut down on repeated prep. After a trial, see whether sharing really helps others and whether the presenters' load has grown. The change isn't just one more word of praise; it's making effort and reward, and responsibility and resources, line up better.
extra:
A family says it wants the kids to enjoy reading, but after every book the only question is what prize they'll get. Outside rewards can sometimes help kids get started, but they can also gradually shift attention to the reward.

You could talk together about what they like to read, let them choose for themselves, and share what they read, rather than turning every book into piecework. There's no fixed reward plan that works for everyone; you need to watch how they actually respond and how things change over time.
steps: Write down the specific behavior you want to encourage, and who has to spend time and bear the cost for it.
Check which current rules actually bring rewards or hassle, and whether they line up with the goal.
Make small adjustments in a transparent, negotiable way, and watch participation, quality, sense of fairness, and long-term side effects.
caution: People are also shaped by values, habits, abilities, and relationships, so not all behavior can be explained as calculation. Rewards can crowd out existing interest, and punishment can lead people to hide things. Goodhart's law focuses on how a measure can become distorted once people chase it; incentives cover a broader range, including consequences that aren't expressed as numerical targets.
exercise: Pick something you wish others were more willing to take part in and write down: "What do they have to give?" "What do they get?" "What do the current rules actually encourage?" Then find one place you could adjust fairly.
brief: Two stick figures complete a shared structure, and specific useful contributions are linked to star-shaped recognition; a magnifying glass checks the link between behavior and consequences, with hints of cooperation and inner motivation nearby.
diagramCaption: From behavior to consequences to the next choice, check what the rules are encouraging. The heart at the top is a reminder that interests, relationships, and values also shape how people respond, so outside rewards aren't the whole story.
